items.followUp: Define an orbital and state how it differs from a shell.

rubric.why: A shell is a principal energy level of an atom.
rubric.description: Defines a shell as a main or principal energy level around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a shell as a main/principal energy level around the nucleus.

rubric.why: A sub-shell is a division of a shell.
rubric.description: Defines a sub-shell as a subdivision or sub-level within a shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a sub-shell is a subdivision/sub-level of a shell.

modelAnswer: A shell is a main energy level around the nucleus in which electrons are present.
A sub-shell is a division of a shell; sub-shells are denoted by s, p, d and f.

items.followUp: State the periodic law proposed by Mendeleev.

rubric.why: Newlands arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic mass.
rubric.description: States that elements were arranged in order of increasing atomic masses.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increasing-atomic-mass order.

rubric.why: The defining observation was the repetition of properties at every eighth element.
rubric.description: States that every eighth element had properties similar to the first.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the every-eighth-element similarity.

modelAnswer: Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing atomic masses.
He observed that the properties of every eighth element were similar to those of the first, like notes in an octave of music.

items.followUp: How many elements are present in the second and fourth periods of the periodic table?

rubric.why: Short periods contain fewer elements than long periods.
rubric.description: Distinguishes short periods by their smaller number of elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that short periods contain 2 or 8 elements (or fewer elements than long periods).

rubric.why: Long periods contain more elements than short periods.
rubric.description: Distinguishes long periods by their larger number of elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that long periods contain 18 or 32 elements (or more elements than short periods).

modelAnswer: Short periods (the 1st, 2nd and 3rd) contain 2 or 8 elements.
Long periods (the 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th) contain 18 or 32 elements.

items.followUp: What is the first ionization energy of an atom? Give its commonly used unit.

rubric.why: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom.
rubric.description: Defines ionization energy as the energy required to remove an electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the energy-to-remove-an-electron definition.

rubric.why: The definition applies to an isolated gaseous atom, and the common unit is kJ mol⁻¹.
rubric.description: Specifies the gaseous-atom condition and gives a valid unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid unit, preferably kJ mol⁻¹; accept electron volt. The gaseous-atom condition may also be credited here.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
Its commonly used unit is kilojoule per mole (kJ mol⁻¹).

rubric.why: Metallic bonding involves positive metal ions in the metal structure.
rubric.description: Identifies positive metal ions as one part of the metallic bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the positive metal ions.

rubric.why: The bond is the electrostatic attraction between the ions and mobile electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies mobile/free electrons and their attraction to the metal ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized/free electrons.

modelAnswer: A metallic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized (free-moving) electrons.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?

rubric.why: Strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions require considerable energy to overcome.
rubric.description: Gives one characteristic property such as high melting or boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid property of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds have several characteristic properties; any other valid property earns credit.
rubric.description: Gives a second distinct valid property of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different property, such as conducting in molten/aqueous form, solubility in water, or being hard and brittle.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: Why does water have a higher boiling point than a non-polar liquid of similar molecular mass?

rubric.why: Water molecules form strong, extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds; alcohol molecules form less extensive hydrogen bonding.
rubric.description: Compares intermolecular hydrogen bonding in water and alcohol.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water has stronger or more extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding than alcohol.

rubric.why: More energy is needed to overcome the attractions between water molecules, raising the boiling point.
rubric.description: Connects stronger attractions to greater energy needed and a higher boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so water has the higher boiling point.

modelAnswer: Water molecules form stronger and more extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds than alcohol molecules.
More energy is needed to overcome these attractions and separate the water molecules, so water has a higher boiling point.

items.followUp: What is meant by the term crystalline solid? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Amorphous solids lack the regular, orderly arrangement of particles found in crystalline solids.
rubric.description: Defines an amorphous solid by the irregular arrangement of its particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its particles are not arranged in a regular pattern.

rubric.why: Examples demonstrate recognition of amorphous solids.
rubric.description: Gives two valid examples, such as glass, plastic or rubber.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two valid examples; accept glass, plastic, rubber or pitch.

modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose particles are not arranged in a regular, orderly pattern.
